nameStory: The 'variegated' in this beetle's name comes from the Latin word meaning 'diversified' or 'having different colors,' referring to its mottled reddish-brown appearance with varied markings. Like other June beetles, adults are most active during June and early summer, emerging en masse on warm evenings. The scientific name 'variolosa' literally means 'having small pox marks,' describing the scattered lighter spots across its wing covers.
description: The Variegated June Beetle is a chunky, oval-shaped scarab beetle with a rich reddish-brown color and subtle mottled markings. These sturdy insects measure just over an inch long (about 2 centimeters) and have the characteristic thick, robust build of scarab beetles. Like other June beetles, they're drawn to lights on warm summer evenings and can be heard buzzing heavily as they fly. Their antennae end in distinctive fan-like clubs that males use to detect chemical signals from females.

idTips.label: Reddish-brown coloration
idTips.description: Rich reddish-brown overall color with subtle mottled or variegated markings that create a slightly irregular pattern across the wing covers

idTips.label: Fan-like antennae
idTips.description: Antennae end in distinctive club-like fans with seven segments; males have noticeably longer, more elaborate clubs than females

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Chunky, oval body just over an inch long with a thick, robust scarab beetle build that feels solid and heavy in your hand

idTips.label: Buzzing flight
idTips.description: Makes a distinctive heavy buzzing sound when flying, often heard before seen as they bump into porch lights on summer evenings

idTips.label: Sandy habitat preference
idTips.description: Found specifically in areas with sandy soils, particularly near coastlines and lake shores where they can complete their underground larval development

habitat: Look for Variegated June Beetles in sandy coastal areas and near large bodies of water throughout New England, particularly along the shores of larger lakes and ocean beaches. They prefer areas with well-drained, sandy soils where their grub-like larvae can develop underground for several years. Adults are most commonly encountered near outdoor lights in coastal communities and lakeside properties.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from sandy soil in late May, with activity increasing as temperatures warm. Look for early individuals around porch lights on the warmest spring evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in June and July when adults are actively mating and feeding. This is the best time to observe them buzzing around outdoor lights or find them on the ground beneath light fixtures in the morning.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down significantly by late summer, though a few stragglers may still be found in early September. Most adults die off as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity; larvae (white grubs) remain deep in sandy soil, feeding on organic matter and plant roots until they're ready to pupate in spring.

funFact: Male Variegated June Beetles can detect a female's chemical signals from over a mile away using their elaborate fan-shaped antennae, which work like tiny chemical radar dishes with thousands of scent receptors.
confusionNotes: Often confused with other June beetles, but the variegated pattern and preference for sandy coastal areas help distinguish it. Remember: 'Variegated by the shore' - this species sticks to sandy habitats near water, while most other June beetles prefer inland areas with different soil types.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'June beetles,' these insects can be active from late May through July, and the name refers to their peak activity period rather than strict timing. The larvae, known as white grubs, spend 2-3 years underground before emerging as adults, which explains why some years have much larger populations than others.
compareHints: As the only Polyphylla species regularly found in New England, compare it with other common June beetles like the Ten-lined June Beetle (which has distinct white stripes) or Brown June Beetles (which lack the variegated pattern and sandy habitat preference). The Variegated June Beetle's mottled reddish-brown coloration and strict association with sandy soils near water make it distinctive among regional scarabs.
